The '''McKendrick–von Foerster equation''' is a linear first-order [[partial differential equation]] encountered in several areas of [[mathematical biology]] – for example, [[demography]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Keyfitz |first1=B. L. |last2=Keyfitz |first2=N. |date=1997-09-01 |title=The McKendrick partial differential equation and its uses in epidemiology and population study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0895717797001659 |journal=Mathematical and Computer Modelling |language=en |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=1–9 |doi=10.1016/S0895-7177(97)00165-9 |s2cid=15550610 |issn=0895-7177|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[cell proliferation]] modeling; it is applied when age structure is an important feature in the [[mathematical model]].<ref name="ref1">{{cite book |last=Murray |first=J.D. |title=Mathematical Biology I: An Introduction |publisher=Springer |year=2002 |isbn=0-387-95223-3 |edition=3rd |series=Interdisciplinary Applied Mathematics |volume=17}}</ref> It was first presented by [[Anderson Gray McKendrick]] in 1926 as a deterministic limit of lattice models applied to [[epidemiology]],<ref>{{cite journal |last=McKendrick |first=A. G. |date=1926 |title=Applications of Mathematics to Medical Problems |journal=Proceedings of the Edinburgh Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=44 |pages=98–130 |doi=10.1017/S0013091500034428 |issn=1464-3839|doi-access=free }}</ref> and subsequently independently in 1959 by [[biophysics]] professor [[Heinz von Foerster]] for describing cell cycles.

==Mathematical formula==
The mathematical formula can be derived from first principles. It reads:{{Equation box 1|cellpadding|border|indent=:|equation=<math> \frac{\partial n}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial n}{\partial a}  = - m(a)n </math>|border colour=#0073CF|background colour=#F5FFFA}}where the population density <math>n(t,a)</math> is a function of age ''<math>a</math>'' and time ''<math>t</math>'', and <math>m(a)</math> is the death function. When <math>m(a) = 0</math>, we have:<ref name="ref1" />

:<math>\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} = - \frac{\partial n}{\partial a} </math>

It relates that a population ages, and that fact is the only one that influences change in population density; the negative sign shows that time flows in just one direction, that there is no birth and the population is going to die out.

=== Derivation ===
Suppose that for a change in time <math>dt</math> and change in age <math>da</math>, the population density is:<math display="block">n(t+dt,a + da) = [1-m(a)dt]n(t,a)</math>That is, during a time period <math>dt</math> the population density decreases by a percentage <math>m(a)dt</math>. Taking a [[Taylor series]] expansion to order <math>dt</math> gives us that:<math display="block">n(t+dt,a + da) \approx n(t,a) + {\partial n\over{\partial t}}dt + {\partial n\over{\partial a}}da</math>We know that <math display="inline">da/dt = 1</math>, since the change of age with time is 1. Therefore, after collecting terms, we must have that:<math display="block">{\partial n\over{\partial t}} + {\partial n\over{\partial a}} = -m(a)n</math>

==Analytical solution==

The von Foerster equation is a [[continuity equation]]; it can be solved using the [[method of characteristics]].<ref name="ref1" /> Another way is by [[similarity solution]]; and a third is a numerical approach such as [[finite differences]].

To get the solution, the following boundary conditions should be added:

:<math> n(t,0)= \int_0^\infty b (a)n(t,a) \, da</math>

which states that the initial births should be conserved (see Sharpe–Lotka–McKendrick equation for otherwise), and that:

:<math> n(0,a)= f(a) </math>

which states that the initial population must be given; then it will evolve according to the partial differential equation.

==Similar equations==

In Sebastian Aniţa, Viorel Arnăutu, Vincenzo Capasso. ''An Introduction to Optimal Control Problems in Life Sciences and Economics'' (Birkhäuser. 2011),  this equation appears as a special case of the [[Sharpe–Lotka–McKendrick’s equation]]; in the latter there is inflow, and the math is based on [[directional derivative]]. The McKendrick’s equation appears extensively in the context of cell biology as a good approach to model the eukaryotic cell cycle.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Gavagnin |first1=Enrico |date=14 October 2018 |title=The invasion speed of cell migration models with realistic cell cycle time distributions |journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology |volume=79 |issue=1 |pages=91–99 |arxiv=1806.03140 |bibcode=2019JThBi.481...91G |doi=10.1016/j.jtbi.2018.09.010 |pmid=30219568 |s2cid=47015362}}</ref>
